name: Chinese Foundation Models
intro:
Chinese foundation models are the large language and multimodal models built, trained, and hosted inside China's regulatory and cloud environment, whether licensed through an API or run as open weights. The category is bounded by origin and hosting, not by benchmark score. It excludes Western models that get compared against Chinese ones in leaderboards, and it excludes the narrower chat apps and vertical copilots built on top of these models. What belongs here is the base and instruction-tuned model layer itself: Alibaba's Qwen (sold internationally as Tongyi Qianwen), Baidu's ERNIE, Tencent's Hunyuan, Zhipu AI's GLM (rebranded abroad as Z.AI), ByteDance's Doubao and Seed models, Xiaomi's MiMo, and MiniMax.

A buyer here chooses along two axes: model capability and jurisdiction exposure. On capability, Qwen is the reference point. Alibaba says the Qwen family has passed three billion cumulative downloads on Hugging Face and now accounts for more than half of global open-weight downloads, ahead of Meta's Llama. On jurisdiction, every tool here carries the same caveat: cross-border data handling and export-control exposure need review before procurement, a risk sharpened by Washington's 2025 reversal letting Nvidia resume H20 chip sales to China, then tighter 2026 curbs targeting Chinese firms operating outside China.

The past year also brought capital-markets validation. Zhipu AI and MiniMax both completed Hong Kong IPOs in January 2026, with MiniMax's stock roughly doubling on debut, a sign this sector now has institutional backing, not just state support.

For most buyers, Qwen is the default reference for open-weight deployment, GLM is the closest thing to a closed-API alternative with an international brand, and Doubao/Seed represents ByteDance's own consumer-to-enterprise model pipeline.

reading.body:
Chinese foundation models have consolidated around a small number of major technology platforms, with ByteDance, Baidu, Tencent, and Alibaba each operating their own large language models alongside smaller competitors.

This concentration reflects the capital and compute requirements that gate entry to foundation model development. Building and operating these systems demands sustained infrastructure investment that only established technology companies with existing data center footprints can absorb. The list does not reveal the underlying compute capacity, power consumption, or physical infrastructure behind each model, so it cannot directly measure the building and power constraints that shape this market.

The uniform data governance note across all seven models signals a structural difference in how Chinese foundation models operate relative to their counterparts elsewhere. Users crossing borders with data face uniform regulatory surface. The data does not explain whether this reflects technical architecture, legal requirements, or operational policy, nor does it cover adoption rates, model size, or performance characteristics that would indicate which systems command the most compute resources.
